```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

## Summary

My original design delimited the centromeres by combining three signals: CENP-A enrichment (ChIP-seq), satellite density and low sequence complexity. When I tried it with public data, the ChIP-seq gave me nothing usable, so I took it out of the workflow. Now I delimit the centromeres by the density of SatI–III satellites only, which is an operational definition. This note explains why, what it changes and what I would need to bring it back.

## 1. The data I had

| | |
|---|---|
| Animal | male `IMCG_204112` (Wu et al. 2024, *Nat Commun* 15:10041) |
| Antibody | Phospho-CENP-A (Ser7) |
| Public runs | IP `SRR29611990` (~80 M read pairs) and input `SRR29611985` (~124 M read pairs), Illumina |
| Used | 2 million pairs of each (the ENA server delivers ~0.5 MB/s per connection) |

## 2. What I found

I mapped the reads to the satellite units and compared the fraction of reads that fell in each family between the IP and the input. If CENP-A were sitting on the satellites, the IP should be enriched relative to the input, with a ratio above 1.

```{r result}
chip <- data.frame(
  family          = c("SatI", "SatII", "SatIII"),
  frac_IP         = c(0.0536, 0.0345, 0.000002),
  frac_input      = c(0.0592, 0.0337, 0.000002),
  enrichment      = c(0.91, 1.02, 0.67)
)
knitr::kable(chip, digits = 4,
             caption = "Fraction of reads in each satellite family (IP vs input)")
```

No family is enriched: SatI gives 0.91 and SatII 1.02. SatIII has so few reads that I cannot interpret its ratio. With 100 to 200 thousand reads in SatI and SatII, I would have seen a true difference of 2× or more.

> I computed these values with an earlier classification of the units, in which "SatII" still included units that I later recognised as SatIII. The conclusion (no family is enriched) does not change, but the per-family figures should not be cited.

## 3. Why I cannot use it to delimit centromeres

There are four reasons. First, short reads fall on almost identical arrays: the satellite arrays of different chromosomes are very similar, so a 150-bp read fits equally well in any of them and I cannot tell which chromosome it comes from. Without that there is no enrichment profile per chromosome, which is what I need to mark where each centromere starts and ends. Second, 2 million pairs are too few to see enrichment peaks, even in the unique sequence on the flanks. Third, recovering it would be disproportionately expensive: I would have to download the full runs (about 11 + 18 GB compressed, ~200 million pairs between IP and input) and map them to the whole genome, keeping only uniquely mapped reads. At ~0.5 MB/s that is more than 15 hours of download, plus compute, to delimit a signal that I already get directly. Fourth, the signal is redundant: satellite density delimits each centromeric block clearly, with sharp edges and no large gaps, and with it I get the lengths I need for H1, H2 and H3.

None of this contradicts the paper. Wu et al. report CENP-A peaks on specific chromosomes (for example, tied to SatII on CHI22, CHI28 and the X), and that kind of result per chromosome cannot be seen with a family-level analysis like mine. I also did not check whether the antibody (phospho-Ser7) alone explains the weak signal.

## 4. What changes for the project

The centromere is now the satellite block with the most sequence in the proximal window, after merging intervals closer than 500 kb. It is an operational definition, not a functional one, so it can be longer than the CENP-A domain. In fact my lengths reach about 10.4 Mb, whereas the paper reports 0.6 to 8.51 Mb for its CENP-A-defined centromeres. I have to declare that my lengths are those of the satellite domain, not of the functional CENP-A domain, and that the scaling results (H1) must be read with that caveat.

## 5. What I would need to bring it back

I would download the full IP and input runs (~29 GB compressed) and map them to the complete genome, which needs several GB of RAM for the index of a 2.9-Gb genome, keeping only reads with a unique mapping (high MAPQ). Then I would compute the IP/input ratio in 10–50 kb windows, look for peaks in the unique sequence that flanks the arrays, compare them with the edges of the satellite block and validate them against the per-chromosome peaks reported by Wu et al.

## 6. What I did with the files

No analysis uses ChIP-seq any more, so I deleted the downloaded reads (`SRR29611990` IP and `SRR29611985` input, ~520 MB) and the enrichment table from my working folder. The values of the result are recorded in section 2 of this note. If I resume the ChIP-seq, the runs can be downloaded again from ENA (BioProject `PRJNA1062519`).
